title: Indian-Origin CEO Pitches Humanoid Robots for US Border Patrol as Pentagon Contract Advances
excerpt: Sankaet Pathak's Foundation has demonstrated its Phantom robot to DHS officials and is negotiating contracts with multiple national security agencies, though no formal agreement is in place.
body:
• Sankaet Pathak, the Indian-origin founder and CEO of Foundation, has pitched his company's humanoid robot Phantom for reconnaissance and surveillance on the US-Mexico border.
  • Foundation has already demonstrated the technology to Department of Homeland Security officials, though DHS says no formal contract or pilot program is currently in place.
  • The company previously secured a $24 million Pentagon contract to develop humanoid robots for military applications through the Defense Innovation Unit.
  • Foundation aims to produce up to 40,000 robots annually by end of 2027 and reduce per-unit costs below $20,000.

From Fintech to Frontlines

Sankaet Pathak is not the most obvious candidate to build robots for the US military. The Indian-origin entrepreneur made his name in fintech as the founder of Synapse, a banking-as-a-service platform. Now, as CEO of Foundation, he is pitching humanoid robots for one of the most politically charged jobs in America: patrolling the southern border.

https://x.com/IntEngineering/status/2090015984824246724

In an interview with Fox News Digital, Pathak said Foundation is in active discussions with multiple national security agencies. "We're in conversations with almost all national security government bodies, so Air Force, Navy, Army, DHS," he said. "We continue to have dialogues. We're starting to negotiate contracts and some applications for them."

"If drones and watchtowers were able to solve for everything, why do we still have humans at the border?"

— Sankaet Pathak, CEO of Foundation

What Phantom Can Do — and What It Can't

Foundation's robot, called Phantom, is designed to navigate rugged terrain, distinguish humans from obstacles, and map its environment autonomously. Pathak envisions it conducting reconnaissance in areas difficult for vehicles, aerial drones, or fixed cameras to cover effectively. The goal is for the robots to flag potential border crossings for human officers rather than make enforcement decisions independently.

The technology, however, remains far from battlefield-ready. The current Phantom MK-1 lacks a battery for extended autonomous operation, cannot function in harsh weather, cannot right itself after falling, and has limited hand dexterity. A more advanced version, Phantom MK-2, is under development with promises of weather resistance, six-hour battery life, and self-recovery capability.

A DHS spokesperson told Fox News Digital that no formal arrangement currently exists. "The Department of Homeland Security currently does not have any non-contractual agreements, pilots, or active prime contracts with Foundation," the spokesperson said.

$24 Million Pentagon Contract

While the border patrol pitch is still in the negotiation stage, Foundation has already secured a significant government foothold. In April 2026, the company won a $24 million contract from the Pentagon through the Defense Innovation Unit to develop humanoid robots for military applications — one of the largest single military investments in humanoid robotics to date.

The company has about 10 Phantom units deployed with clients, including an Atlanta automaker and two consumer goods manufacturers. Foundation has also inked approximately $10 million in government contracts. The company is closing a funding round reportedly surpassing $100 million at a valuation trending toward $3.5 billion, according to sources cited by Newsweek.

The Broader Race for Military Humanoids

Foundation's push comes amid growing interest from defense establishments worldwide in humanoid robotics. China is actively pursuing similar technology, and Russia has deployed ground robots on the Ukraine front. The BBC reported that Foundation claims to be the only US-based firm currently building humanoid robots specifically for a broad range of defense applications.

Pathak envisions thousands of humanoids deployed across the US within 12 to 18 months for niche tasks, scaling to hundreds of thousands in five years, and millions within a decade — handling everything from defense logistics to domestic applications. Foundation aims to produce up to 40,000 robots annually by the end of 2027 and eventually reduce costs to below $20,000 per unit.

What's Next

The intersection of immigration enforcement and autonomous robotics is certain to draw scrutiny from both sides of the political aisle. Civil liberties groups have already raised concerns about the use of surveillance technology at the border, and the deployment of humanoid robots would add a new dimension to that debate. For Pathak, the pitch is straightforward: robots can go where humans struggle to, reducing risk to Border Patrol agents while extending surveillance coverage. Whether Washington agrees — and whether the technology can deliver on its promises — remains to be seen.
